utterances.text: And do you know about the killing, once again of an Albanian, Naser Hajziri in Mitrovica in December 1998 in the Melica cafe?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This case was mentioned earlier when I was talking about the person who killed him and is serving a sentence in prisons in Serbia, somewhere in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the command structures of the KLA adopted a decision to assassinate prominent Albanians loyal to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that is something that was written in a report by the Kosovo Verification Mission for the period ranging from the 9th to the 12th of March? It was contained in that report, that fact.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know something about the killing of three Romany? They were brothers; Gani Gushani, Basra Gushani, and Hilmi Gushani, three Roma brothers who were killed in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about this case and I have the original report which I passed on the following day to the media, but that murder, the case of those murders again is a mystery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, they had reported to -- they wanted to become local policemen and put their names up for that position and then they were killed. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about this. Whether they wanted to join the police or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you that they were killed the next day, after they had put their names forward for becoming local policemen. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said he knows nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember when there was a kidnapping, the deputy of the Kosovska Mitrovica municipality, Ajeti, was kidnapped. Do you remember that? He was the head of the local police, too, in Kosovska Mitrovica. And he was kidnapped in 1998, and nobody knew of his whereabouts but it was supposed that he had been murdered. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard about the fact that he is missing, he has disappeared, but I've always suspected that these mystery killings have been organised by the Serb secret services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are suggesting that the head of the local police force, an Albanian in Mitrovica, was killed by Serbs? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that, and I don't know anything about that, but I know that he was the director of the Mitrovica prison. But other things other than that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He used to be the director of the Mitrovica prison, that's true. So he was employed by the state and was, I'm sure, highly respected, a highly respected state official. And I quoted from the OSCE report, so there you have it. I think matters are clear on that point. Do you know, on the 27th of December, that three members of the KLA killed the Potparol [phoen] of the Romany Gypsy organisation?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's contained in the OSCE report too. And what about the 2nd of January in Radasnik? Radasnik is part of Mitrovica, isn't it? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time that I hear about such a location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not a place, it's part of Mitrovica. But anyway, two Serbs were killed, one of them a journalist.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no Radasnik in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for that Radasnik as part of Mitrovica and the two Serbs, one of whom was a journalist, that is something that the OSCE report talks about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm thinking this: That a more efficient way of putting this information before us may be to produce the report in due course, the OSCE report. It may be that the Prosecution have got a copy of it. You can ask this witness questions, but there seems little point if he's going to answer he doesn't know anything about it. Have we got -- Mr. Nice, can you help us with that? Have you got a copy of that report?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's being looked for at the moment. It's obviously not in court at the moment, but if I've got it, I'll produce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking these questions because I think it is quite obvious that I'm asking this with respect to the witness's credibility. He knows nothing. He knows nothing about a single crime committed over the Serbs or loyal Albanians. He knows nothing about anything that was done by the KLA, and he claims -- and he claims what he claims, that the Serb army and police force went and ran after civilians in the midst of the Shala Operative Zone, with 4.000 KLA members present. So forgot about these 4.000 and just concentrated on the civilians. That's why I am asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Have you got any more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know on the 12th of January another Albanian was killed, the owner of a bar? He was taken out of his bar and shot outside on the 12th of January, 1999, once again in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please mention the exact location where that happened? Because I'm once again saying that there is no place named Radasnik in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't. I never assumed -- I'm not talking about Radasnik now. I'm talking about the Albanian who was killed and who was the proprietor of a bar. He was taken outside of his bar and killed by a group of KLA members. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to know the location of where the incident happened and then I can talk about it, if I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just answer this: Do you know of any occasion about this time in which an incident of that sort happened?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about such an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, in March, a Serb who was shot at and riddled with bullets underneath a bridge in Kosovska Mitrovica? And there are not many bridges, I don't suppose, in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On March of what year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible for him to have been killed by the Albanians, because all the streets and roads were filled, packed with police, military, and paramilitary Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about this Serb who was killed. Do you suggest that that was done by a Serb unit too?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about this murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, then, about something that took place on the 12th of March? That was quite a bit before the aggression. On the 12th of March, when the director of the theatre was killed? He was also an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true, and the director of the theatre was not killed because I am the director of the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not the director of the theatre you but the Albanian who was the director of the theatre. I'm talking about him, not about you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was there another director of the theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was, and he was a Serb, and he is alive. One clarification, Your Honour, if I may. If we are talking about Kadri Kadriu, he was one of the managers of the cultural house in Mitrovica. He was arrested on the 11th of March, and he was shot on the 13th of March in Trepca, near the mine. He was shot and he was mutilated. He was one of the managers, Albanian managers of the cultural house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The main director, whether he was the principal director or one of the directors, that's not important. What I was talking about was an Albanian who was killed. Do you know that a judge, also an Albanian, was kidnapped, a lay judge, in fact and that, on the 15th of March, the KLA informed his family and said that he was being held in Shala? He was a lay judge, an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about such a case, and I'm sure that it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That is also something that exists in documents. And then we come to the 18th of February, when another Albanian was kidnapped in Shala. You know nothing about the abduction of Albanians during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be useful to know who are we talking about by name and surname, because I have a list of all the cases -- of all the cases that happened in Mitrovica, and I have them with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about an incident on the 18th of January? On the 18th of January, are you aware of the next incident when a rocket was shot -- targeted a jeep towards Stimlje, on the road towards Stimlje, and five people were injured who were in the jeep? Do you know about that attack by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the case very well, but I don't know who shot the jeep because I know that the jeep hit the wall and then spun around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what would you say? What do you think? Who attacked the police at the exit to Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who carried out the attack, but if we are talking about the case that you mentioned, I know that the jeep hit a high wall and then it overturned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of another event that took place on the 20th of January, 1999, when the police surrounded a house in Mitrovica in which there were between 10 to 15 members of the KLA? On the 20th of January. Do you know about that incident?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about this case, but this did not take place in Mitrovica but in the village of Vaganice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... about that incident. Vaganice, as you yourself said, is not even three kilometres away from Mitrovica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. And on this occasion, two members of the KLA were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the police, on the 20th of January, surrounded that particular house in the presence of the OSCE observers, that the OSCE observers were present on the occasion when the event took place?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about this incident, but I have been myself with the observers of the European Union, and that was the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. In the presence of the OSCE observers, it is true that two were killed and -- KLA members were killed and the others escaped. And in the report, it states that the KLA opened fire on the policemen first, as incidentally, was always the case, but it just happened that the OSCE observers were present on this particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that I was not there on the day of the incident, but I went to the scene the following day with OSCE observers. We went there to the scene of the incident the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You talked about demonstrations on the 27th of March, 1989.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 7th of March but on the 27th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 27th of March, 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said the 27th. I did not say the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not waste time on that. March 1989, demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who led these demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The demonstrations were led by the students and the teachers themselves and, later, the whole of the population - I mean the Albanian population - joined in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that these were destructive demonstrations, that everything was broken, shattered wherever the demonstrators passed by?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true because the demonstrations were taking place in a location where there was nothing to destroy but there was only a bridge which is known as Ura e Gjakut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All the shop windows were broken, all the stores, everything that was nearby. Don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well the demonstration of the 27th of March, 1989, but it is not true what the accused is saying because the location where it was taking place was not surrounded by anything other than the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they moved nowhere? They didn't go anywhere from the bridge?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not move because the road leading into the city was blockaded by the Serb police, and they had no chance of getting into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now you've come to the main point. Why do you say the Serb police?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Serb police fired and killed Albanians, because there was also Albanian police at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that it was precisely at that time and at these demonstrations in Mitrovica that the majority of the policemen were Albanians?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know pretty well, but it was Serb forces from Vushtrri and Leposavic who came there, and Albanians were on the second line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know even in which line the Albanians were?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know it very well because I was at the gas station near the bus station, and I saw them lined up. And I know them. I used to know them, even in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But my question is very precise: Do you know that the majority of the policemen at these demonstrations were ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the demonstrations we are talking about, the majority were not Albanians but Serbs, because new forces were deployed there, saying that the Albanians didn't help the Serb police and so the Serbs were put on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is your explanation. Unfortunately, it is not correct. But let us go on from here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this is interesting because the witness is saying that five Albanians were killed and the Prosecutor said that 100 Albanians were killed in these demonstrations, and now we've come to a figure that is 20 times lower. But even what the witness has been saying now is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put a question. If you have a question, Mr. Milosevic, put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I have questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to move on from the demonstrations to yet another subject. Do you remember a decision of the Albanian political leaders that Albanians should boycott their work? Do you remember the word "boycott" and the decision to carry out this boycott all over?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true, and it's groundless, because the decision of the Albanians was that not a single Albanian should leave their work without being forced to. This was a decision taken by the independent union of Kosova, headed by Hajrullah Gorani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that Albanians did not go on strike and did not stop working and did not state that they would not carry out their work duties?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should not confuse things. The strike is one thing and work is another thing. You said that it was a decision not to go to work, that is, to boycott work. This is not true. As to the strike, it's something else. It was a one-day strike, and Albanians, some of the Albanians, participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about a one-day strike. I'm talking about a long-lasting boycott of work duties.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there was no boycott because it was the insistence of all Albanians not to leave the job without being forcibly asked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that Albanians went to work and that they actually worked those days and those weeks?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the doors of the factories and plants were blocked by the Serb police and they did not allow them to get inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was forbidden to enter the premises?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanian workers were forbidden to enter the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know full well that this is not true, and you know that for a long time there were orders to boycott work. And you claim, therefore, that all of that is incorrect; right? That all of this is not true?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is incorrect. The truth is that the Albanians were recommended not to leave their work without violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any case of violence over anyone in any institution or any company? Is that perhaps your assertion?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were policemen placed at the doors of the factories, plants, who did not let the Albanian workers go inside the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember the strike at Stari Trg?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well both strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that it was actually the other way around, that the strikers who, for political reasons, had taken over the job places, the workplaces, actually blocked these workplaces and did not allow workers who wanted to work to come in at all? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question, and not a couple of questions at once but please only one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that strikers blocked workplaces and remained there and did not wish to work?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well. But they blocked the workplaces, it was a hunger strike, and they asked the resignation of three officials of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now you said that they blocked workplaces. They blocked workplaces. And this went on for days. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strike went on for eight days, until the workers were promised that these miners of Trepca, that everything will be improved and the resignation will take place. They were lies. And this is why the workers left the mine and came out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Your claim is that it was eight days. Let us say that it was eight days. Do you remember that for all these eight days, three times a day, in three shifts, workers who wished to work came in but they were not allowed in because the others had blocked the workplaces? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true at all, because the entire Albanian population of Kosova solidarised with the miners, the strikers in Trepca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is also not correct. Do you remember the structure of the entire Kosovo leadership at that time precisely? In 1989, that is.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the structure"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for the main political offices in Kosovo, were they held by Serbs or Albanians? Who held the main political offices in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were held by the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these Albanians, did they support these destructive demonstrations or these blockades of workplaces that you refer to? You call this blockades of workplaces so let us use your terminology. Did they support that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no destruction inflicted, and I didn't say that there was a blockade of workplaces. And the leadership of Kosova did not support them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you claim that the other Albanians did support them.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in full solidarity with the Trepca miners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A short while ago, you claimed that there were no Albanian policemen and in 1989 there were Serb policemen only in Kosovska Mitrovica, and now you say that all Albanians expressed their solidarity with those who blocked workplaces. So do you remember, did you at least watch this on television, that shift of workers would come to work but they could not enter the workplace because it had been blocked, things like that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a couple of questions. Please take them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's try and bring this to a close. I think we've dealt fully with this. What he suggested was that a shift of workers tried to enter the workplace but couldn't do so because it was blocked. Now, is that right or not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't even see this on television?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said it's not right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask him another question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the Serbs, at least, who had jobs there? Did they want to work there or not?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't want to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even the Serbs didn't want to work there?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't go to the plants. Since they didn't go, I presumed they didn't want to. We are talking about Trepca here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But a short while ago, you explained that only Albanians supported this blockade of workplaces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't remember him being asked that. Did only the Albanians support the blockade? Just a moment. Just a moment. Did only the Albanians support the blockade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many Serbs were then employed at Trepca?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the relevant bodies might give you the exact figures. I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can give a yes or a no answer to this: It was a political strike and the blockade was for political reasons; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a strike which asked for the resignation of three politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us not go into further detail. Obviously, there are material facts involved and there is no reason to debate that here. Let us look at this statement, this declaration that was brought here as some kind of a crown document. I'm asking you now, whose declaration is this? Is this a declaration of the work organisation of the medical centre of the 13th of July, basic organisation of hospital services in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a decision which they had to sign, all the Albanian workers of the General Hospital of Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it only Albanians who were employed at the Mitrovica hospital?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also others, not only the Albanians. But only the Albanians were offered to sign such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, in that medical organisation, everybody together, all the employees, Serbs, Albanians, took upon themselves the obligation to sign a declaration stating that they would carry out their work duties at the workplace?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if the Serb workers were offered this statement, they had the reason to sign it because they recognised Serbia as their own republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we have come to your main point now. This is, therefore, a declaration that is required by a hospital which is state owned; right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is state owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that declaration, it says that one should take upon the obligation that during working hours, working hours, "I shall abide by legal provisions, notably the law on labour relations."

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But at the end, it writes that, "I recognise the Republic of Serbia as my own republic." This was why the Albanian staff refused to sign it, because they didn't consider it their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't say here I admit or recognise or do not recognise Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 1286 to 1296. something that is obvious. It says, "will abide by the regulations of the republic." "Abide by the regulations in their republic." Now, what is controversial about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us have the exhibit, Exhibit 24. Put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you comment. Mr. Nice, how was this translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a draft translation, I think, provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if it's a draft translation it will have been by somebody working in the Office of the Prosecutor, and then a final translation will come available in due course. Incidentally, it is a document, I said, the original was available if we wanted to look at it, and I have that at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The original of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The original of this document. I said yesterday it was available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps that should be given to the witness. And the Cyrillic could be put on the ELMO, please. Now, Mr. Milosevic, what was the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point was that in any state, in a state company, in a state hospital, and even in a private company or in a private hospital, a person who is employed there during working hours has to abide by the law. And it says here that they will abide by all regulations, and we are going to get to this controversial part as well, because I see that this law on the use of language and alphabet is something that the Prosecutor particularly pointed out. It's the other way around, it's not the way you've put it. That they would observe regulations and laws during working hours. Tell me, please, what is controversial about this, that a person who is employed somewhere and receives a salary there should observe laws and regulations during working hours, laws that are passed by that republic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph which is regarded as controversial. Now, have you any questions to the witness about this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can barely see this, so I have to look at the transcript. That was precisely my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we get the white copy on the ELMO, and if the witness looks at the green, it might be easier to see it. The Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I have the Cyrillic copy. It's right over here. I don't need it on the ELMO. Perhaps you do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. Put it on. Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, could you read the second paragraph so we could have a translation of it. Are you in a position to do so, to read the Cyrillic, the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see here written "original in Serbian." Can I say the translation? "I accept the Republic of Serbia as my own republic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. What I wanted you to read was the entire second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but it is difficult for me to read in Cyrillic letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have to await the final translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read it for you. I'm going to read it in Serbian, this second paragraph, and very slowly at that, very slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I also declare that during working hours, I shall abide by the provisions of system-based laws of the Republic of Serbia, notably the law on employment under special circumstances, law on territorial organisation, the law on the use of language and alphabet, and other laws that pertain to the established territorial integrity and sovereignty of my Republic of Serbia in which I live and work." Full stop. No more than that. Therefore, the republic, according to the Yugoslav Constitution and according to its own Constitution, is a state. It passes laws. There is not a single law that pertains only to Serbs or only to Albanians or only to Hungarians or only to Ruthenians, Romanians, Bulgarians, or anyone else for that matter. That is to say, laws that are passed by the republic - since you are legal people, you know this full well - they apply to all citizens, and this is an organisation per se that made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, we have taken the point you make. Now, have you any more questions for this witness about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is: What's wrong with this document? What does the witness consider to be a problem in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has given his evidence about that, and it's not for him to take the matter further. You can make submissions in due course and we will have to decide what the effect of those submissions are and what the effect of this document is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do have other questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We're going to adjourn now. Now, we shall expect you, Mr. Milosevic, to finish your cross-examination of this witness this afternoon. You will then have had up to four hours to cross-examine. So perhaps you would organise your cross-examination to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't worry. I shall certainly finish today by all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half past two. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Barani, before Mr. Milosevic continues, I wanted to ask you, and you may have given this evidence already: When was the declaration that we're looking at issued? The declaration that had to be signed by workers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of 1990. In other words, 1990, 1991. You can see on the declaration itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And it was issued in the same form, in the same language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was issued just as it is. That's an original declaration that was given to the staff of the Mitrovica General Hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the time by which I promised to finish today, before I continue, I nonetheless do have to ask several questions to clarify some points that remained unclear. I didn't read through the locality, the word locality carefully, the locality where two Serbs were killed, one of the journalists -- where one of the journalists were killed. The locality, the place was called Rasadnik.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Fidanishte where there was a well-known case of where the bodies of two Serbs were found in which the international observers who were in Mitrovica were at the scene of the incident and took notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And something in connection with the theatre. There were two wings of the theatre, the Serbian drama theatre and the Albania drama theatre. You were director of the Albanian drama theatre.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were not two theatres in Mitrovica. From 1992 there weren't. There was a group that worked in the Serbian language, but they didn't do very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say there were two theatres. What I meant was within the frameworks of one theatre house there was the section for Serb plays, a Serb play section and Albanian play section. That was what I meant.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three sections operating in the same building; Albanian, Serbian, and Turkish, but the Serbian and Turkish sections didn't work, but the Albanian theatre, which I headed, did work and still works and did so without interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's a very positive thing. That's good. And I'm not bringing that into question at all. But at all events, the work of the overall theatre was financed by the municipality. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group that I led was never financed but merely the hall in the culture centre was placed at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The municipality placed the hall at your disposal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every now and then. Many plays were also put on in the city park, and I have photographs of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you weren't the director of the theatre but the Albanian play section. The fact that the Turkish and Serb part didn't work, wasn't working, I didn't ask you anything about that. Next, you said that all Albanians except for the leadership, during the blockade of the work posts, supported the strikers, and I have received the following information: Not even in Mitrovica, where the strike was the largest, the post office, the health institutions and services, or the courts or the state administration, none of these stopped functioning, along with a series of other public services where the Albanians worked as a majority. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been the occasional Albanian who worked during the strike, but the overwhelming majority of Albanians were on strike and expressed their solidarity until the last day, which was 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I am speaking about the large majority of Albanians in all public services - the post office, banks, and all the other things that I mentioned - that they did go to work. They were working. Now, do you recall that the director of the bank in Mitrovica was also an Albanian? His name was Jusuf Gjosha and the SDK social accounting service director was Jashar Ismaili, also an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the directors were at this time, but I do know that the great majority of the Albanian population kept order and expressed their solidarity with the Trepca workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I have presented facts that speak of the contrary being true, but you say that that was not so. Have I understood you correctly? Do you consider that that is not true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I asked him whether he considered that that was not true. The witness, with respect to the declaration and in a negative context, spoke about the use of language having to do with law, so I go back to the declaration once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why was there a problem with the law on the use of language?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly what problem is in question here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is the following: In commenting on the declaration which you -- and you can't explain where the problem was, you mentioned the law on the use of language, which is mentioned in the declaration, because it says, "law on the use of language and alphabet," and you brought this up when you were speaking. Now, how did you see -- what problem did you see with respect to the law on the use of language? Where was the problem there, according to you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that I mentioned any law here ever, because I don't know what the rules are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about it. You were commenting the declaration that we read a moment ago, before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why not ask him: Mr. Barani, was there any difficulty as far as you were concerned, as far as you could see, in the declaration which is that, during working hours you would abide by various laws, and that included the law on the use of language and alphabet? Could you see any problem in making such a declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only problem when in signing this -- in signing this declaration is signing where it says, "I recognise the Republic of Serbia as my own."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where does it say that? Could you quote it, please, in the declaration, the exact words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him have the declaration in front of him. Mr. Barani, can you read it? And it refers to the territorial integrity and sovereignty. You can read that, can you, in the Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem reading, and I can't read it all in Cyrillic, but I can see where -- I can see where it says, "my republic of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And yes. And where is the word "I recognise" that is the key word? "I accept."

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all a bit earlier, but at the end, it says, "my Republic of Serbia." And for this reason, the Albanian workers didn't sign it. This -- here it is. This is where it is written. This is the original document. You can all see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who else can bring in laws other than the legal organs of Serbia, legislative organs of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanians have never recognised the Republic of Serbia as theirs. That's the whole issue about this declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that you claim that Kosovo is not in Serbia. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Kosovo, even today, is in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise Kosova as Kosova outside Serbia and not part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you understand that an independent Kosovo is only a dream, flying on the wings of NATO bombers, and once they fly away, you'll wake up and be in Serbia again? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to answer that question. It's a comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to another question. You claimed that the demonstrations were peaceful ones, and I said that they were destructive ones. And at those, as you yourself said, peaceful demonstrations in 1989, a policeman was killed by the name of Miroljub Tanaskovic precisely at the gas station, the petrol station, that you were at. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that on the 27th of March a Serbian policeman was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, can those demonstrations then be referred to and called non-destructive, peaceful demonstrations if that was so?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, the place where the demonstrations took place didn't have any houses or shops nearby, and there are still none there today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where they began, yes, but where you moved around, no; and you did move around and destroyed everything in sight. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is 27th of March, 1989, it's not true. It's as I say it. In that place, that place has not changed at all, and nor in the town. Demonstrators couldn't enter the town because police were stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did they kill this policeman then?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the policeman was killed. I have no knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's sufficient for this. You spoke yesterday about the 13th of March, in particular, when, at the marketplace, bombs exploded. You even, as I jotted down, said that the Serb policemen threw bombs at the marketplace. And now I'm going to ask you the following: Do you remember that on that occasion in the marketplace in Mitrovica, a bomb exploded and that at the same time the same type of bomb exploded in Podujevo? And as far as the victims are concerned, four citizens were killed and 30 others were wounded in Kosovska Mitrovica, seven of them seriously wounded. The victims were both Serbs and Albanians. So at the same time, these bombs were planted in the marketplace in Mitrovica and Podujevo, and according to the findings of the Verification Mission of the OSCE --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him answer the question. Were there bombs -- were there bombs also placed elsewhere that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no knowledge about other places, only about Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not only was a bomb planted in Podujevo, but it exploded at the same time. In Mitrovica and Podujevo at the same time. And in the report which the observers compiled, it states that the bomb was a homemade bomb. That means that it was an explosive device planted by terrorists simultaneously in Mitrovica and Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Barani, Mr. Barani, do you know anything about the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, and I have the names and the surnames of the victims, and there were not four but seven and more than 90 were wounded. And I collated into information together with the OSCE who were at that time in Mitrovica. All the wounded were in the Mitrovica General Hospital, and I got all the notes about the wounded from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was a television report from the hospital after the planting of those bombs, that we saw those sorry people, the casualties, lying there in hospital, both Serbs and Albanians?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw any television broadcast about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the four dead and 30 wounded, I got those figures from the report that was drawn up by the observers themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about the killing of a group of intellectuals on Dren mountain; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- this was not murder but their arrest, and the fate of two of them is not known to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the fate of those two is not known. You said that it took place on Mount Dren. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me. There are two or three there; give me one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that it took place on Dren Mountain?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place is called the village of Dreth, and there is a mountain of the same name and it is in Zubin Potok municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In fact, it's on Mokra Gora mountain, which divides the Zubin Potok municipality from the Srbica municipality. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place I mentioned belongs to Zubin Potok municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about others, but from what you said, from your testimony, I gained the impression that these people, this whole list of some 23 individuals, were killed. That's the impression I gained. And you now said that the fate of two of them is -- only two of them is not known. So could you clear that up? Are you talking about 23 people or two people? And then I'll continue once I get that clarification from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that was his evidence in chief. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a question of 23 of a group of 25. Twenty-three disappeared, and their fate is not known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I understood what you said quite correctly. You said, in connection with that, that they came across an ambush, came upon an ambush placed there by the army or the police, that they were ambushed by either the army or police.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said. According to those who survived and escaped arrest, one of them is Xhafer Behrami, from the village of Kotorr in Skenderaj municipality, who was a member of this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think it's logical for the army or the police to set up an ambush for 20-odd civilians? Does that seem to you to be logical?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's not really a question for the witness. That's what he says, whether it's logical or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. I claim that it was an armed group of the KLA, that they bore arms.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true. None of them had weapons, and none of them were members of the KLA. They were all teachers, doctors, technical workers, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a group of intellectuals, and now we have from 17, 20, 27, 21, 17, 17, 31 and so on and so forth. So apart from two or three persons, all of them were military-able men, and they were all males. That's obvious, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said they weren't members of the KLA, and they didn't have weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, he claimed that he just saw the KLA in passing, and later on, we established that he knew all the commanders. This is another thing that he is claiming now. He was a theatre director, but this is such -- these are such great contradictions that you can't get away from them. But let me move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that 5.000 people were sent and imprisoned in Smrekovnica. It is between Mitrovica and Vucitrn.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said 5.802 in Smrekovnica prison and in the secondary technical school that was an improvised prison in -- near Mitrovica, and from there, they were sent to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the warden of that prison in Smrekovnica was in fact an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the prison in Smrekovnica is a regular type of prison or, as we call it, a correction centre?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it's a prison and, at this time, it was a notorious prison among the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the capacity of that prison, whose warden was an Albanian, and, as you say, it was an infamous one, notorious one, as you said, that the capacity of prisoners was 300 to 400 inmates at most?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that very well, but that -- you have in the statement the period between which the number I quoted, over 5.000 of Albanians were imprisoned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am precisely stating that that is impossible, in view of the capacities of the prison, and that you are speaking untruths.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true, and I have statements from all those who were held prisoners when they came back from Albania, and they reported to the office for the Protection of Human Rights and prison -- and Freedoms, and they explained in detail all what they suffered in the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You mentioned an improvised prison, is that right, in a secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim that it is untrue that anybody forced civilians into prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that this is not true? We are now going to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For you, it is untrue also in 1990 when --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can he repeat the figures, please, for the interpreters? Can the witness repeat the statement, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the figures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that for the accused and his clique, it is no doubt impossible that 7.200 Albanian school pupils were poisoned in 1990 on 21st and 22nd of March and also the 19th and 20th of April, and I have films of the poisoning with me and the statements of more than 100 primary and secondary pupils.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This uni-ethnic poisoning of yours was well-known throughout Yugoslavia. This is not exactly news. And now I'm asking you in relation to that, do you know that both Serb and Albanian children sat in the same classrooms and then it was claimed that some kind of gas was being released that poisoned only Albanian children on ethnic grounds?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you say is not true, because awhile ago the pupils were segregated and the Serbs were studying in the morning, whereas the Albanians were going to the school in the afternoon. And I say this with full responsibility, because on the 12th of April, 1990, in the elementary school Nondabulka [phoen] in the Iber neighbourhood, the teachers and the pupils of the school had a bottle filled with a kind of substance, and I personally got hold of that with, the late Professor Latif Berisha and Vehbi Zeqiri. We all sent it to the Council for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms in Pristina. We handed that over to Zenun Celaj, the secretary of the council. The same sample was sent to France ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Barani, we must stop you. We are going some way now from the subject matter of the cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should say so, too, especially in connection with this farce that all of Yugoslavia is familiar with in relation to this poisoning. You are here as - how should I put this? - somebody who brought a sensational document, a document that went from hand to hand, and this is a list of reservists from the village of Svinjar. We saw it here.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: About which list are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this one that was given to you so that you could authenticate it, the list of reservists from the village of Svinjar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit 28. Let the witness have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it. I've got it here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We don't really have to waste time with this. It's been displayed several times by now.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list of the paramilitaries from the Frasher village of Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything else you want to ask about it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, is this what you asked for? Is this the original that you wanted to see? I have a copy, of course, but this is the list. It says "List of the reserve force of the village of Svinjar." That's what you wanted to see, right, in the original?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this? I would like to hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list, with all the names that it contains, has been found in the village of Frasher at the checkpoint where the Serb paramilitary were stationed before the arrival of the NATO troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What do you think it represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It contains the names and surnames, and at the beginning, it says it's the list of the Serb paramilitaries for the village of Frasher i Madh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here from the village of Svinjar, and I don't know which village you have it from. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the village of Frasher, formerly Svinjar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Oh, I see. Now you have new names. Now it's a different story. Where does it say that this is a list of paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very start, it writes that it's a list of the paramilitaries, and we consider paramilitaries those who -- who you call reservists, military reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A person remains speechless in face of this, but let us clarify one point: Do you know that every Yugoslav citizen who had done his military service was a military reservist?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, the list was found in the place where the Serb paramilitary were stationed in the village of Frasher, where all the Albanian houses were burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, I would like to clarify this list which you consider to be a document. So could you please answer my questions. Do you know that every citizen of Yugoslavia who had done his military service is a military reservist and is registered in military records as a military reservist according to the profession that he was involved in while doing his military service?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list was found at a place where serious crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could have found John Galsworthy's books at the crime site. So how can you bring the two together? I don't understand what this means, this list of reservists from the village of Svinjar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've exhausted this topic now. We have the document, and the parties can make comments about it. You can make comments, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, every citizen of Yugoslavia who had done his military service is a reservist and is registered in the list of military reservists in the register. Here it says on the top, "List of reserve force from the village of Svinjar." In the English translation, it says "Reserve forces." There is nothing to do with reserve forces. This is not correct. These are reservists. This is a list of military conscripts who may be mobilised but do not have to be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is their list and nothing else. The only figure -- the place of employment is needed because of the law. If somebody was mobilised, called up as a reservist, that means that the federal state has to compensate his company for his salary, because the company cannot pay him while he is away, and that is why it is quite clearly stated where each person works so that this payment can be made accordingly. So this is just an ordinary list of military conscripts from a village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have the point. Now, what he's put to you, Mr. Barani, is that this is a list of conscripts. Forget the name of the village. Forget what's written at the top. But as far as you can see, is there anything inconsistent in it being a list of reservists with their employment mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the Serbs who operated during the wartime, that's why the names of their professions is written by their names, because they were paid for having served as such forces during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it seems to me we can't take this any further. Can you move on to the next topic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this could be of any assistance, perhaps we could give lists of several hundreds of thousands of military conscripts that every village and every street in Yugoslavia has. Several hundreds of thousands of persons were mobilised during the NATO aggression. It's as if you were providing the telephone directory, as a secret document at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You keep referring to paramilitary formations. I claim that we did not have paramilitary formations. We only had the official army and police. A short while ago, you explained that everybody who was mobilised from the reserve force was a paramilitary, in your opinion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your forces were distinguished by the uniform they had, the three of them; the paramilitaries, the police, and the soldiers. Although they swapped the uniforms and there were multicoloured ones, but what we considered as paramilitaries, they never changed their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who you consider to be what, but I claim that there were no paramilitary forces. On the contrary: There were orders from the Supreme Command that every paramilitary unit should be disbanded and arrested immediately. Therefore, reservists cannot be considered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're not here to give evidence now. You can do that in due course. The witness has given his answer. Let's move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is taking up a lot of my time, his extensive answers, and I have to see whether I should shorten something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor put a question when saying that they were told that they should go to Albania. The Prosecutor asked, "Who told you?" The witness did not answer that. The Prosecutor went on and said, "What were you told?" And the answer he got was that they were told to go to Albania. I'm going back to the Prosecutor's question that he did not respond to. Who told them to go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the army, the police, and the paramilitaries who ordered them and forced them to go towards Albania after their houses were raided and looted and they were forcibly evicted. I'm saying this in accordance with all the statements of thousands upon thousands of Albanians from Mitrovica and from the rest of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If reality could be created through statements, it would look different than it looks today. Let us move on to another document now that was found underneath some boards, and it was presented here as a revelation, something that was discovered under very special circumstances, and these are very plain lists of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th Platoons, and the addresses and the telephones of these persons are provided and that is only logical for, say, the company commander to have if somebody gets killed or something happens to such a person that the family can be identified. These are the names of soldiers in the 1st and 2nd and 3rd Platoons respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the value of this document that they had such difficulty in obtaining? This document contains soldiers' names and their home addresses. What is the value of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter which we will have to decide in due course. But have you got any questions for the witness about it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it has to do with the fact that he brought it as some kind of proof. What does this prove other than, for example, that John Doe lives in such-and-such a street and that his telephone number is such-and-such and they're going to call his mother there and notify her at that address that he got killed if he gets killed. In any army anywhere in the world, every soldier would give his address if something happens to him so that his next of kin may be notified. So what do you prove by this name and address?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: What is the value of this document in the opinion of the witness? Because he's the one who brought it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a question for the witness. We're going to have to determine what value it has, and no doubt the Prosecution will address us on it in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to the Prosecutor's question as to how many houses and shops of Kosovo Albanians were destroyed or set fire to, you said 9.550. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not. We're not talking about the houses of Kosova, but it's just for the Mitrovica municipality, and that's 9.540. And we have complete documentation, documents with -- accompanied by pictures and all the statements of those involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. You said that that was the figure; right? All right. Do you know how many Serb houses, shops, and all the rest that you have registered in respect of the Albanian victims were burned down, destroyed, and looted? Do you have figures in that connection?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have figures related to these facts because some Serbs, as they left their houses, they set them on fire, whereas we got evidence from people whose families, members of families have been killed and their houses were burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim, therefore, that the Serbs, as they were leaving their houses, set fire to their own houses by themselves; right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said partly. According to many witnesses. If it wasn't like that, they would not burn them, but they would stay there until they reached some agreement with their owners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So again, through your witnesses, you are proving that Serbs set fire to their own houses and to Albanian houses in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment. Yes. You don't have to answer that. He's answered that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I shall move on to the next subject, but please give short answers and do not describe incidents that you have already described, because my time will run out. You have said that Latif Berisha, president of the DSK Mitrovica, on the 24th of March, around midnight, that somebody barged into his house and they took him out and killed him and that these people were masked Serbs. How come you know that these masked persons were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The daughter of Latif Berisha, who is a teacher of Albanian language and literature, Fatime Berisha, at 1130, 2330, after the murder, called the chairman of the Presidency, Ismail Katiqi, and informed him of the murder, and he informed me afterwards, and she was in the room when the Serbs entered and took the late Professor out and shot him in front of his own door -- house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they were wearing masks. How come you know they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know because the people of the place where his house is still -- still is - it's in ruins now - used to be inhabited by Serbs, with the exception of four or five Albanian houses who never dared leave their houses during the wartime until the Serbs came and forcibly evicted them from their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. All right. Thank you. Thank you. You do not know whether they were Serbs. You said that Agim Hajrizi, president of the trade unions, that he was also killed by Serbs. How come you know that it was Serbs who killed him?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because his -- he, Agim, Adem Hajrizi's mother and his 11-year-old daughter were killed. His wife was at home with two other children. They left. They got on the roof and waited there until the murder was ended, was committed, and she gave evidence to the court and people are being tried for that murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And does the witness know -- do you know how many colleagues of yours, officials of the political party DSK that is headed by Ibrahim Rugova, were the victims of political clashes and were the victims of the terrorists of Hashim Thaci, to put it more precisely? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said even earlier that I think that all the victims or such mystery cases of murders have been perpetrated by the secret Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Then you can answer my following question: How come Rugova's functionaries are being killed now since there are no more Serbs from June 1999?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that there are no Serbs in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's another matter altogether. But how come after June 1999 -- 1999, who is it that is killing Rugova's functionaries? Do you consider that it is still the Serbs who are doing that? Do you still consider that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's first establish that the witness accepts your proposition that the functionaries are being killed now, insofar as this is relevant. Now, do you -- wait a moment. Do you accept this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some were killed, but that doesn't necessarily mean that they are functionaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read out a few names: Raci Ismet from Klina, president of the municipal board of Rugova's party in Klina. Then Shaban Manaj from Istok, the president of the municipal board of Rugova's party in Istok. So that means local party heads, the heads of the Rugova party in Klina and in Istok, those two examples. Then we go to Ismet Hajderaj from Pec, member of the Presidency. Mustafa Xhemail is the next one, from Pristina, member of the main leadership of Rugova's party. Then we have Xhemail -- Xhevat Makolli, a close associate of Rugova's, also killed. Muharem Jakupi, also a functionary in Rugova's party, the DSK, who was also killed. Do you know that this is being done by Hashim Thaci to weaken Rugova and to frighten his supporters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A list has been put to you, Mr. Barani, and it's suggested that these -- the names on it are the names of people who have been killed, and it's also suggested that they were functionaries of Mr. Rugova's party. Now, there are two questions there. Perhaps you can deal with them. If you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partially. Some of the names I know, I know, and I know about their murders. But as I said earlier, people are being held responsible for certain murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've taken that point as far as we can. Yes. Have you anything else now for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, during the war, an assassination attempt was made on life of Rugova himself?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I think it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was guarded by our own police force to prevent him from being killed?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that he came to see me and that I sent him and his entire family to Italy with nine family members of his for me to be certain that Hashim Thaci wouldn't get at him and kill him, Hashim Thaci and his terrorists?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the media, I have become informed that Ibrahim Rugova is in Belgrade, but I don't know anything what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I have already asked you about how you personally stuck up the lists of Serbs to be executed on the library building and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard what the witness said about that. That is not what he said. We're not going back over it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said he placed the names of the perpetrators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... please. Move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have given us a document of some kind, and you say of that document that it is a list of Albanians which should be summarily liquidated.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the list and this is what it said at the heading, that we have submitted to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Are you conscious of the fact that this document is a forgery?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I clearly indicated where I found and from whom I got it and that two, three persons in the list that I have submitted to this Court are already shot now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you speak Serbian well?
