utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, you probably aren't in a position to know that this document could not have been written by a Serb. I'm going to ask you a few questions now about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have the exhibit out. Exhibit number 27.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, I'm drawing your attention in particular to the fact that in the translation, these obvious, blatant facts -- there are blatant facts that indicate that the document was not written by a Serb but you can't see this because it's been translated without going into those facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the original, too, plus a photocopy of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the original in the Cyrillic script. First, no Serb says "specialno" -- but says "specijalnu."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: With a "j", interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when he goes to a doctor, a specialist, everybody knows that he's going to a "specijalist" with a "j" and not to a "specialist" just "i-a". And this is a mistake that no Serb would ever make but it is a mistake that many foreigners make, especially Albanians. They make that particular mistake. Secondly, when you say "specialno jedinici" for -- referring to a unit, no Serb would say that. He would just say "specijalnu jedinicu."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The case is wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But most Albanians would say for a "specialno jedinici."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: So the case is wrong again, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now what it should have said is "specijalna jedinica," with a "j" and not without a "j". All the mistakes that have been made in these few words are so obvious that there is no child going to elementary school which would make the same spelling mistakes in the Serbian language as have been made in this document. Secondly, it says, "List of Siptars Who Should be Summarily Liquidated." First, the word "pod" has been translated as "po," meaning "accordingly." The word "p-o-d," "pod" and "p-o," "po" have two quite different meanings, and once again, no Serb would write this. "Pod," the word "pod" means "underneath" and not "po," which is "accordingly"... "summarily." The "p-o" would be a different word. So there's just one difference between those two words. Like the difference between the sounds in lawyer and liar. The difference is just in one sound or letter, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What you have said is very interesting. But you have just given quite a lot of evidence. You must bring evidence to substantiate what you just said. You can't give the evidence. I hope you understand me, and I hope that in your defence you will be adducing evidence to substantiate what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the piece of evidence itself. Everything that I said is written here. This is the proof and the evidence. It says "specialno jedinici."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you said about the Serbian language and why it is not a genuine document. You need to adduce evidence as to that. You're not a witness. You're conducting your -- you're conducting your defence, and you may put certain questions to this witness, but you cannot give evidence in this way, and I would expect that you would adduce evidence in your defence at a later stage to substantiate all of what you have said, and that would make it much more credible to the Chamber. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more flagrant example, referring to this text that you have submitted as an exhibit. It says "likfidirati". That is something -- it is common knowledge that only somebody speaking German would use the "v" -- the "f" instead of a "v." In this case, it was an Albanian-speaking German. There is not one single Serb who would write "likvidirati" with an "f" instead of a "v."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think it's time for a question. The suggestion appears to be that an Albanian -- I'm sorry. Yes, an Albanian-speaking German wrote this document. Now, Mr. Barani, can you help as to that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I said I don't know the Cyrillic language, and the document was found by Ramadan Kelmendi in the communal house of Mitrovica after the war. It contains 66 names, as you can see for yourselves, three of whom have already been killed. I can't give any other explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please bear in mind the fact that never, ever would a document, since Yugoslavia has been in existence, could a document of this kind be issued by any kind of organ or institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is your evidence, Mr. Milosevic. Now, move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there are not only these points but there are essential contradictions which illustrate the fact that this is a forgery. But never mind. You can judge this anyway you want. All I want to say is that I'm impressed with the triumphant attitude with which this was presented by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it doesn't mean anything or, rather, it does. It means a forgery. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where, when, and to whom did you make statements about this whole case? Because -- these are three questions. Would you answer each individually. Where, is the first one, when, and to whom, the three questions, did you make statements about what you have been testifying?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. When did you first make a statement about this particular case and to whom and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the first time when I laid hold of this document that you have in front you, I informed the council in Pristina. Then, at a later phase, when ICTY investigators came to Mitrovica, I attached this particular document to my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When was that, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was 2001. I can't give you a precise date when the investigators came there. Maybe it was July, August. I can't give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said 2001, when the ICTY investigators came to Mitrovica to collect statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: August 2001, is that it? Was that your first statement, the first statement that you gave to the representatives of this indictment of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have made many statements on the war, so I can't remember each and every date. But this particular one I remember because I made it to the last investigators -- the investigator who came to Mitrovica in 2001. I can't give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you give any other foreigner, investigator before that, any statements?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many organisations that were interested in such cases, I have also shown this document to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Various organisations. But you gave the investigators a statement on the 20 something -- 20 of August, at least 2001. August 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: July, August must have been - I don't remember the date - 2001, the last investigator that came to Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the accused would take the opportunity to read the statements, I can give you the dates from them. The interview with the ICTY investigator were on the 25th and 26th of August, and the statement was signed on the 1st of September of last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just drawing your attention to the fact that in the indictment raised in May 1999, statements were taken in August of 2001. And generally speaking, I'm drawing attention to the way in which all this was being done. I shall be finishing in a little while. Just like NATO used terrorists in the war, this false indictment is used for KLA witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Milosevic, you must stop making speeches and just ask a question or we shall stop here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We only have a few issues to take up with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Mr. Barani, yesterday you gave evidence about an incident at the Friday marketplace on the 13th of March, 1999, in Mitrovica. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: All right. You told the Court that it was Serb police who caused the explosion of bombs at the marketplace. You were questioned about that by Mr. Milosevic himself. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: One question that was not put to you and I will put to you now: Were you there when these bombs were ignited and exploded, and how do you know it was the police?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statement, I said that three shells were dropped from the police and the army from the Zvecan e Vogel village, and I was just filming and photographing Kadri Kadriu, a well-known Albanian painter who was shot dead by the Serb police a few days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Meaning you were present?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present at the scene, but I heard whistling from the place when I was at the mosque, and later on, I heard the detonations, one after the other. Later, I learned that it had all happened in the market, in the marketplace. I went out. I saw two workers, and we entered and then we got onto a car which was accompanying the funeral, and we went to Suhodoll i Poshtem village where he was buried. I gave the bag where my camera was to a friend, and I went across the garden nursery and I went to my office which was in the neighbourhood Qendra 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. When questioned by the Prosecution about the actions in Bair - or Bair, I don't know how you pronounce it - on the 26 or 27th of March, 1999, it was put to you that you observed what happened with the old paralysed woman and the two old men. Were you there or was this incident reported to you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there, but it was reported to me later, two days later. It was reported to me that four Albanians, three elderly men and one woman, were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let me move on to your evidence on the two murders in the 7th of September neighbourhood of Mitrovica. You told the Court about the murder of three or four members of the Alushi family on the 28th of March, 1999. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well. There were four members of the Alushi family, the two sons of Alush Alushi, his brother, Fehmi, and his son. They were shot at the yard of their house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't need to repeat what I put to you. Let me ask you the question. Am I right in thinking you said murdered by the Serb police, and if so, how do you know? Were you present or was the incident reported to you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that they were -- they were killed by the Serb police but by plainclothes Serb civilians. And it was reported to me that -- by people who were there and who saw the scene, and I attended the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Mr. Barani, you have been reminded that you gave an earlier statement to an investigator of the ICTY last year in August, and you said you remember that. Is that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no interpreting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. You gave -- you were reminded that you gave an interview to an investigator of the ICTY in August last year; is that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to ask you, would you describe fighting, clashes, and killings between the KLA and the Kosovo authorities in 1998 and 1999 as war?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me. Are we talking about any killings?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Fightings, clashes, and killings between the KLA and the authorities of Kosovo. Would you describe that as war?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On -- about these cases, about any killings, I have no knowledge about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let me read you a quote. According to your statement given in August last year, you said, and I quote: "When I'm talking about the start of the war in Kosovo, I would mean it started on the 26th of November, 1997. On that date, the first bullet was fired back from an Albanian against the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I repeat the question. Would you describe fightings, clashes, and killings between the KLA and the authorities of Kosovo in 1998 and 1999 as war?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous statement, I said that the first shot was fired on the 26th in Vojnik, which is part of the Skenderaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That does not answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Evidently he is not understanding. You consider that, Mr. Barani, to have been the start of the war, the firing of that shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consider it as the beginning of the war, because from after that date, immediately on the 28th, during the funeral of a teacher which was killed by the Serb police, members of the KLA appeared openly, and from then, the war did not end up until the peacekeeping forces entered Kosova. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... he considers that war. If you have another question, you can put it but it is rather technical.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think it is, but it clarifies what I could not find in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I've got a further question, Mr. Barani. Did you have a weapon in the spring of 1999, and if so, did you carry that weapon with you when you were travelling around in the area?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- my only weapon was the camera, the pencil, and the video camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I deal with a few matters quite quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Mr. Kelmendi from whom you obtained a document you've been asked about, the document in Cyrillic, is he still alive, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's alive. He lives in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that you provided this document, or you've been asked questions about providing this document to another organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have here what is, as it were, the original that we have. The document is said to be a forgery. If the witness would like to identify whether it's the first or second generation of the document, then maybe it's a document that the Court would like to retain, as the allegation of forgery has been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would just like to look at it and tell us about. Could you just look at this document, which I think you may have brought with you when you came here. Is this the very document that was given to you by Mr. Kelmendi or was it something that was copied from the document given to you by Kelmendi, or can you not now be sure?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that this document that this document that I'm holding was given to me by hand by Ramadan Kelmendi. It's the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you can hand that to the usher. That can stay with the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we not seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that you've necessarily handled the original itself because you had a photocopy to go on. But in any event, now that it's asserted it's a forgery, it's good for the original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It will be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While I'm dealing with witness statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the accused should see that document which you've just produced. There is a question of time. I would ask the interpreters if we could sit a bit later. Some indulgence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not many minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the witness is looking at that, I observe my learned friend's, the amici's comment about the invalid woman. I checked the record. I certainly didn't put it that he observed something himself. The question was put neutrally about her. As to statements, can I simply, rather, at this stage for convenience, inform the Chamber that, in addition to the witness's statements to the ICTY investigators, others of his statements to the International Coalition for Justice and to OSCE have already been disclosed to the accused weeks and months ago. Can I deal with another administrative matter arising from cross-examination without wearying you with any detail? The OSCE report comes in two volumes of this size that I'm holding up. There will be OSCE witnesses called. The status of the report is, of course, entirely uncertain at the moment. I don't know one way or another whether we will seek to put the report in. Probably not in its entirety for that would be a very substantial document to lay before you being the conclusions of another. Whether parts of it will be, as it were, adopted and dealt with in evidence, I don't know. The document is available but its status is probably something that ought to be considered quite carefully, given its overall nature. As to the cross-examination -- as to the cross-examination on the basis of that report, and I'm not going to take you through the various passages, but it would be my submission that the cross-examination has been extremely selective and it will be necessary to look at passages in full to take value from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the lists, I wonder if you could help us with this, please, Mr. Barani. We've seen two lists, in each case all names end in "I-C," in "-ic" ending. Is that a name ending of Albanians or not?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which names are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The list of soldiers, for example, that all end in "-ic." Is that an Albanian name ending or not, or is it not significant?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That applies to both lists, as the Court will recall. Again, just as a matter of checking the record, the witness was asked, in relation to the declaration about employment, what he had said about the significance of the reference in the declaration to language. In his evidence, he did not ascribe any significance to that at all in his evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a general point, Mr. Barani: It's been suggested to you that you are not telling the truth to this Chamber about your level of knowledge of crimes by the KLA. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about crimes committed by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just in general. It's been suggested that you are not being truthful about your level of knowledge, having been asked questions by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding crimes committed by the KLA, I have no knowledge of any being committed by an army which I only know of was out there fighting for the protection of their own people from their total extermination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have three more questions, I think. The man Kadriu, the Albanian theatre manager, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom was he killed?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is again a mystery murder, but it is presumed that at the time when he was killed, which was the 13th when he was found dead in Stari Trg, near the mine, and mutilated - his right ear was cut off - it is presumed that he was killed by the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another matter of detail. Your Honour, there was a suggestion that the revelation by this witness of his having been theatre director is a revelation. It is in his witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two last questions. You were asked about listing names in the library beside a list of -- names of perpetrators beside a list of those killed. At the time that you listed those names, were Serbian police inquiries into the deaths of Albanians being conducted in a thorough-going way?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I opened that exhibition at the city's library in Mitrovica, I had the pictures of those who were killed and mutilated put up. At the same time, many names of those who have perpetrated crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The question is: At that time, to your knowledge, were Serb police investigating the deaths of Albanians in a thorough-going, in a thorough way?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge that there has been such a thing. I'm talking about investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Last question touches on something that you dealt with in earlier evidence, but this: You spoke in cross-examination of handing your reports from time to time to the media. The word used was "the media." To whom did you make your reports with your findings available in the media?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talk about handing reports to the media, I'm talking about the papers in Kosovo, Radio Deutsche Welle, and the Voice of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Contemporaneously; that is, at the time of making those reports?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I handed over copies of the reports, but the original was retained with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hand those reports over at the time, at the time of events and at the time you made the reports?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On many occasions, the report was written just hours after the incident, but in other cases, it was written up two days later, immediately after I received statement -- statements from witnesses. And then as soon as the report was written, was handed over simultaneously to the media. And I have all the -- possession of all the copies of these reports with the details of who committed the crimes, the killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was just one supplementary question I should ask relating to an earlier question I did. As to Albanian names, are you familiar yourself with Albanian surnames in the Presevo valley? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Barani, you said today, early in the morning, that during the 15th and 17th of May, 1998, you had some official meetings with KLA commanders. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, but that was after the 15th and the 17th, but not in September 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sixteen Albanians were dead. Sixteen Albanians were dead?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the killing of the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. My question is what do you mean by official? In what capacity did you attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in these meetings as the president of the Council for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Later on, you also testified that you met them, the members of KLA or commanders of KLA, when you passed by the village of Vaganice. What do you mean by "passed by"? Wasn't it that you went to Vaganice specifically for the purpose of meeting them?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't going there to meet them, but as I was passing by to -- to find out about the situation in other villages, what was happening in other villages. But I have not gone specifically to Vaganice to meet the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If my memory's correct, I remember that you said that you got the -- some information from members of KLA on what was happening around the region. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we were talking about the region of Shala and not about the village of Vaganice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you also give some information to the KLA members about what you collected and information?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BARANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not interested in what information I had initially, but I continued to collect information which was interesting to me, which I was interested in, in order to compile the reports and then pass them on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Barani, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is there something else you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just something I wanted to mention, possibly immediately after the witness has withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The videotape is running out. Can you deal with it in one minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. All I was going to say is that it's forecast that the first witness tomorrow will be a witness who will give evidence in fully closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's probable that the evidence of that witness will last the full session, but it may be two. There are some associated matters of a procedural nature that should be dealt with and, by order of the Court, have to be dealt with themselves in closed session, but it's only in relation to those matters that, at our application, the Court will be in closed session. It would, of course, have been difficult -- I think the Court knows the issues. It would have been desirable to have dealt with them today, if possible, but if we've run out of time, it's not possible, it will have to be tomorrow..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have to deal with them tomorrow. Very well. Half past nine tomorrow, please. Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.18 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 1st day of March, 2002, at 9.30 a.m.
